title: Cell type versus reversible cell state
open: Determine which molecular differences define persistent neuronal or glial types and which reflect reversible activity, metabolic, developmental, or disease states. A solution should predict longitudinal identity and state transitions under controlled perturbations.
status: Whole-mouse-brain and adult-human-brain transcriptomic atlases greatly expanded classification in 2023, but static molecular clusters do not themselves resolve this distinction.
why: Establishes what a cell census should count and which classifications support causal experiments.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Functional proteome beyond the transcriptome
open: Construct matched measurements of RNA, protein abundance, protein localization, modification state, and physiology in identified cells. Determine which additional molecular layers materially improve functional prediction.
status: The 2023 brain atlases establish transcriptomic and regulatory reference points; a transcript count is not a measurement of localized functional protein.
why: Resolves discrepancies between molecular classification and actual cellular behavior.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.

title: Physiological functions of synaptic condensates
open: Determine when phase-separated synaptic assemblies are necessary for vesicle organization or plasticity in living brains. Perturb phase behavior separately from protein concentration and binding affinity.
status: Synapsin–vesicle phase separation was demonstrated in 2018; that result does not by itself establish the full in-vivo causal role.
why: Distinguishes a mechanistic organizational principle from an in-vitro analogy.
key_works: Milovanovic et al. (2018), *A liquid phase of synapsin and lipid vesicles*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5671`.

title: Molecular identity of synaptic tags
open: Identify the molecular states that mark specific synapses for later capture of plasticity-related products, including their lifetimes, specificity, and reset mechanisms.
status: Synaptic tagging was experimentally established in 1997; identifying a complete, context-general molecular implementation remains open.
why: Explains how a neuron directs broadly produced resources to selected synapses.
key_works: Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Synaptic memory despite molecular turnover
open: Determine how a particular synaptic modification survives replacement of its constituent molecules. Demonstrate a maintenance mechanism that predicts both persistence and selective erasure.
status: Multiscale synaptic models provide favorable retention properties, but their biological state variables and renewal mechanisms remain to be established.
why: Addresses the mismatch between molecular lifetimes and memory lifetimes.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Dendritic computations actually used during behavior
open: Determine which nonlinear dendritic operations are necessary for particular natural behaviors, rather than merely possible under controlled stimulation.
status: Human cortical dendrites exhibit powerful nonlinear computations ex vivo; their deployment during ordinary human behavior is not established by those experiments.
why: Tests whether neurons should be modeled as single units or structured computational networks.
key_works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Poirazi, Brannon, and Mel (2003), *Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network*, DOI: `10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00149-1`.

title: Myelin’s timing versus metabolic contributions
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Separate myelin-dependent changes in conduction from changes in axonal metabolic support, and quantify their respective contributions to learning and long-term survival.
status: Learning-related myelination is causally implicated, but disrupting myelin-related processes can affect several functions simultaneously.
why: Determines which myelin functions therapies must restore.
key_works: McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`; Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.

title: Branch-specific axonal transmission reliability
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Measure when an action potential successfully invades every branch of an identified axon during natural activity, and predict branch-specific failures or timing changes.
status: Dense connectomes establish branching geometry, but anatomical continuity does not establish reliable, state-independent transmission to every terminal.
why: Tests whether an axon broadcasts one identical message to all targets.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`.

title: Predictive developmental wiring code
open: Predict which individual neurons will connect from lineage, molecular recognition, geometry, and developmental activity. Validate predictions after altering one component of the developmental program.
status: Modern cell atlases and connectomes provide endpoints, but they do not constitute a generative developmental wiring law.
why: Connects developmental biology to mature circuit architecture.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`.

title: Context-specific necessity of gliotransmission
open: Determine which astrocyte populations release transmitters under physiological conditions and when that release is necessary for circuit computation or behavior.
status: A specialized glutamatergic astrocyte population was reported in 2023; this does not establish universal glutamate release by astrocytes.
why: Resolves a major mechanistic dispute without treating astrocytes as a uniform class.
key_works: de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.

title: Synapse-specific selection for elimination
open: Identify the combination of activity, complement, surface signals, and microglial state that determines whether a particular synapse is removed or spared.
status: Complement-dependent elimination and activity-dependent microglial pruning were established in 2007–2012; a predictive synapse-by-synapse selection rule remains open.
why: Enables targeted preservation or removal of connections.
key_works: Stevens et al. (2007), *The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2007.10.036`; Schafer et al. (2012), *Microglia sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity and complement-dependent manner*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.026`.

title: Reconciling sleep-dependent clearance measurements
open: Reconcile apparently conflicting sleep-clearance results using matched tracers, compartments, behavioral states, and transport models. Distinguish tracer entry, redistribution, and actual elimination.
status: A 2024 study reported reduced clearance during sleep and anesthesia; a 2025 study implicated sleep-related vasomotion in glymphatic clearance. The assays and mechanisms require direct reconciliation.
why: Determines whether proposed clearance therapies target the correct process.
key_works: Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Noninvasive human clearance quantification
open: Develop a validated, repeatable human measurement of brain solute elimination that does not depend on invasive tracer administration and distinguishes relevant compartments.
status: Mechanistic animal studies and anatomical drainage discoveries provide foundations, but their measurements are not automatically transferable to routine human monitoring.
why: Makes clearance hypotheses testable in longitudinal human studies.
key_works: Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`; Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`.

title: Learning without symmetric feedback weights
open: Establish when biologically realistic asymmetric feedback can support accurate multilayer learning, and identify conditions where it provably cannot.
status: Feedback alignment and inference-based learning supply partial computational solutions; their biological implementation and general guarantees remain open.
why: Tests whether a central obstacle to biologically plausible learning is fundamental or architectural.
key_works: Lillicrap et al. (2016), *Random synaptic feedback weights support error backpropagation for deep learning*, DOI: `10.1038/ncomms13276`; Song et al. (2024), *Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01514-1`.

title: Genuine neural criticality versus statistical lookalikes
open: Distinguish true critical dynamics from noncritical systems that produce similar avalanche distributions through subsampling, filtering, or external drive.
status: Neuronal avalanches were reported in 2003; power-law-like observations alone do not settle the underlying dynamical regime.
why: Tests a major proposed organizing principle of neural activity.
key_works: Beggs and Plenz (2003), *Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003`.

title: Predictive coding versus alternative mismatch mechanisms
open: Design interventions that distinguish explicit prediction-error computation from adaptation, movement feedback, and other mechanisms producing mismatch responses.
status: Sensorimotor mismatch signals were reported in mouse visual cortex in 2012; the response alone does not uniquely identify a predictive-coding architecture.
why: Tests a widely used explanatory framework with discriminating predictions.
key_works: Keller, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`; Rao and Ballard (1999), *Predictive coding in the visual cortex: a functional interpretation of some extra-classical receptive-field effects*, DOI: `10.1038/4580`.

title: Causal selection of one speaker in a crowd
open: Identify how attention selects one speaker’s representation while preserving the ability to switch targets, and determine the causal contributions of auditory and control circuits.
status: Selective cortical representation of an attended speaker was demonstrated in 2012; a representation does not itself establish the selection mechanism.
why: Explains a central limitation of real-world hearing.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`.

title: Reliable human cochlear-synaptopathy diagnosis
open: Develop a noninvasive marker that quantifies cochlear synapse loss in an individual and predicts specific hearing difficulties independently of other auditory damage.
status: Mouse work established lasting neural degeneration after apparently temporary noise-related threshold changes in 2009; individual human quantification remains a distinct challenge.
why: Makes otherwise hidden injury measurable before major threshold loss.
key_works: Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`.

title: Nonlinear perception of odor mixtures
open: Predict when mixtures are perceived elementally, configurally, or suppressively from component identity, concentration, and prior exposure.
status: Single-molecule perceptual models and receptor-interaction studies supply pieces of the problem; mixture perception is not reducible to averaging component descriptors.
why: Most natural olfactory environments contain mixtures.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`; Fukutani et al. (2023), *Antagonistic interactions between odorants alter human odor perception* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Motor cortical dynamics-to-muscle commands
open: Determine which dimensions of motor population activity causally generate muscle activation and which reflect preparation, feedback, or correlated internal state.
status: Rotational population dynamics were demonstrated during reaching in 2012; descriptive dynamics do not by themselves identify the output-generating mechanism.
why: Connects population models to physical movement.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; Michaels, Dann, and Scherberger (2016), *Neural Population Dynamics during Reaching Are Better Explained by a Dynamical System than Representational Tuning*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005175`.

title: Cerebellar credit assignment for delayed outcomes
open: Identify how cerebellar plasticity associates an outcome with the relevant earlier activity when delays exceed a simple coincidence window.
status: Reward expectations are represented in cerebellar circuits; the temporal eligibility mechanism linking them to particular synapses remains a separate question.
why: Explains learning in temporally extended real-world actions.
key_works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`.

title: Joining local maps into global knowledge
open: Explain how separately learned spatial representations are aligned when an animal discovers a connection between environments, including inconsistent or ambiguous correspondences.
status: Place-code dynamics demonstrate representational flexibility, but do not specify a general map-merging algorithm.
why: Explains flexible route planning and discovery of shortcuts.
key_works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`; Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.

title: Physiological-state-dependent value
open: Explain how thirst, hunger, fatigue, and other bodily states transform the value of outcomes and the willingness to work for them.
status: Thirst circuits can anticipate physiological consequences, and dopamine signals distinguish aspects of motivation; a unified state-to-value computation remains open.
why: Connects homeostasis to flexible decision-making.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Redundant mechanisms of social attachment
open: Determine how attachment persists when a proposed signaling pathway is absent, distinguishing developmental compensation, redundant circuitry, and context-dependent necessity.
status: Oxytocin-receptor knockout prairie voles retained social attachment in a 2023 study, challenging simple claims of universal receptor necessity.
why: Prevents overgeneralizing a single molecule into a complete social mechanism.
key_works: Berendzen et al. (2023), *Oxytocin receptor is not required for social attachment in prairie voles*, Neuron; PMID: `36708707`.

title: Cellular variables that generate sleep need
open: Identify the quantities accumulated during wakefulness that causally generate sleep pressure, and determine whether different cell populations track different needs.
status: Clearance and vascular studies establish processes linked to sleep, but none alone establishes the complete variable that makes sleep necessary.
why: Distinguishes causes of sleep need from processes that happen during sleep.
key_works: Xie et al. (2013), *Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1241224`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Human enteric functional diversity
open: Determine which molecularly defined human enteric populations perform distinct sensory, motor, and secretory functions and how those functions vary along the gut.
status: The 2020 atlas identifies candidate populations; direct human functional assignments remain a separate experimental program.
why: Enables cell-selective treatment rather than broad modulation of gut activity.
key_works: Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Complete magnetoreception mechanism
open: Identify the in-vivo receptor, physical transduction process, neural pathway, and behavioral readout responsible for magnetic orientation in a defined species.
status: Migratory-songbird cryptochrome 4 showed magnetic sensitivity in 2021 experiments; this is not a complete receptor-to-navigation causal chain.
why: Would connect a subtle physical effect to a verified sensory system.
key_works: Xu et al. (2021), *Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9`.

title: Toxic tau species and causal propagation
open: Identify which tau assemblies cause neuronal dysfunction, which mainly mark disease, and which processes are necessary for spread between cells.
status: Human Alzheimer tau filament structures were resolved in 2017; structural identification does not establish that every observed assembly has the same toxicity or propagation role.
why: Makes anti-tau interventions target the relevant species and processes.
key_works: Fitzpatrick et al. (2017), *Cryo-EM structures of tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/nature23002`.

title: Durable benefit from dopaminergic cell replacement
open: Establish long-term, controlled clinical benefit from replacement dopamine neurons, including stable integration, appropriate regulation, and protection from recurrent pathology.
status: A 2025 phase I hES-derived dopaminergic-cell trial is an important milestone; early safety and feasibility do not settle durable comparative efficacy.
why: Tests whether cell replacement becomes a reproducible restorative treatment.
key_works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`.

title: Broad functional restoration after spinal cord injury
open: Restore coordinated mobility together with sensory and autonomic functions across diverse injuries, rather than demonstrating a single assisted motor task.
status: The 2023 brain–spine interface restored walking in a proof-of-concept setting; general recovery across people and functions remains open.
why: Targets the full burden of spinal injury.
key_works: Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: Adult-like maturation of human neural organoids
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Produce organoids with validated adult-like molecular, electrophysiological, metabolic, and plasticity properties without equating one maturation marker with adulthood.
status: Organoids model aspects of development, and transplantation improves maturation and integration; fully validated adult-like equivalence remains a separate target.
why: Enables better models of adult disease and physiology.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Simultaneous whole-brain cellular recording in behaving mammals
open: Record relevant fast activity across an entire mammalian brain simultaneously, with quantified coverage and perturbation of normal behavior.
status: The 2025 brain-wide mouse map aggregates extensive recordings across animals and sessions; it is not simultaneous cellular recording of one whole brain.
why: Resolves coordination that cannot be reconstructed reliably from separate sessions.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: R10.03. The approximately 150-CAG transition in Huntington’s neurons
open: Determine whether the reported transition near 150 somatic HTT CAG repeats represents a causal biological threshold, a distributed set of cell-specific thresholds, or an apparent boundary influenced by sampling and selective cell loss. Predict the transition from repeat length, interruption structure, cell identity, and age.
status: A 2025 single-cell study linked extensive somatic expansion to loss of striatal projection-neuron identity, with a marked transition around 150 repeats in the sampled cells. That result should not be treated as an invariant threshold already established for every neuronal population or patient.
why: Would turn repeat measurements into mechanistically grounded estimates of proximity to neuronal failure.
key_works: Handsaker et al. (2025), *Long somatic DNA-repeat expansion drives neurodegeneration in Huntington’s disease*, PMID: `39824182`.

title: R10.04. Suppressing MSH3 without exchanging repeat expansion for other genomic damage
open: Define a tissue-specific and time-dependent intervention window in which reducing MSH3 meaningfully suppresses pathogenic repeat expansion without unacceptable accumulation of other DNA errors. Success requires measuring both repeat stabilization and broader mutation burdens over extended periods.
status: In 2025, antisense-mediated MSH3 suppression reduced somatic CAG expansion in Huntington’s disease patient-derived striatal neurons. Long-term genomic safety and the necessary degree of suppression remain separate questions from demonstrating reduced expansion in culture.
why: Establishes whether a promising repeat-expansion intervention has a usable long-term therapeutic margin.
key_works: Bunting et al. (2025), *Antisense oligonucleotide–mediated MSH3 suppression reduces somatic CAG repeat expansion in Huntington’s disease iPSC–derived striatal neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.adn4600`.

title: R10.06. Replacing damaged neuronal nuclear pores without opening the barrier
open: Determine how aged neurons inspect, repair, and replace damaged components of exceptionally long-lived nuclear pore complexes while preserving nuclear selectivity. Establish whether defective pores can be selectively renewed without transient leakage or wholesale disruption of nuclear transport.
status: Extremely long-lived nuclear pore proteins were identified in rat brain in 2012. Component longevity does not establish that pores are immutable, nor does evidence of component exchange by itself explain safe replacement of damaged assemblies in old neurons.
why: Provides a specific intervention target for deterioration of nuclear compartmentalization.
key_works: Savas et al. (2012), *Extremely long-lived nuclear pore proteins in the rat brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1217421`.

title: R10.07. What information the axon-to-cilium serotonin synapse conveys
open: Determine whether serotonin delivered to a neuronal primary cilium carries instructions distinguishable from serotonin acting on the rest of the cell. Selectively disrupt the ciliary route while preserving nonciliary signaling, then test predicted changes in nuclear regulation and behavior.
status: An axon–cilium serotonergic synapse and a cilium-to-nucleus signaling pathway were demonstrated in 2022. The anatomical connection and chromatin effects are established findings; their behavior-specific informational role remains the narrower target.
why: Could reveal a dedicated channel through which particular inputs regulate long-term cellular programs.
key_works: Sheu et al. (2022), *A serotonergic axon-cilium synapse drives nuclear signaling to alter chromatin accessibility*, PMID: `36055200`.

title: R10.08. Reissner-fiber mechanics versus urotensin signaling in spine morphogenesis
open: Separate the contributions of Reissner-fiber tension, motion, biochemical interactions, and cerebrospinal-fluid-contacting neuronal signaling to maintenance of body-axis shape. A solution should predict which deformities follow selective mechanical disruption versus selective interruption of the downstream signaling pathway.
status: Reissner-fiber-dependent urotensin signaling was linked to prevention of spinal curvature in 2020. A September 2025 preprint reported that motile cilia rotate a tensioned, anchored fiber, adding a mechanical mechanism that must be integrated with the signaling results.
why: Connects nervous-system fluid mechanics to a concrete developmental orthopedic phenotype.
key_works: Lu et al. (2020), *Reissner fibre-induced urotensin signalling from cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons prevents scoliosis of vertebrate spine*, DOI: `10.1242/bio.052027`; Bearce et al. (2025), *Motile cilia spin the Reissner fiber, a tensioned and anchored extracellular thread essential for body morphogenesis*, preprint, DOI: `10.1101/2025.09.25.678623`.

title: R10.10. Physically consistent, independently validated chloride microdomains
open: Establish when neighboring neuronal compartments genuinely maintain different free chloride activities, rather than different sensor environments, pH, or chloride-binding conditions. Derive and test the transport, buffering, and geometrical requirements for the measured gradients to persist.
status: A 2021 study reported chloride microdomains associated with heterogeneous GABA responses. The remaining challenge is independent quantitative validation and a transport model that explains the gradients’ stability under realistic diffusion and activity.
why: Determines whether a single intracellular chloride value is an inadequate description of inhibitory signaling within one neuron.
key_works: Rahmati et al. (2021), *Unique Actions of GABA Arising from Cytoplasmic Chloride Microdomains*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3175-20.2021`.

title: R10.12. Homeostatic compensation in axon-carrying-dendrite neurons
open: Explain how neurons whose axon originates from a dendrite stabilize excitability when their axon initial segment lacks the homeostatic plasticity observed in comparison neurons. Test whether compensation shifts to dendritic conductances, inhibition, synaptic scaling, or another compartment.
status: A study published online in 2024 and in a 2025 journal issue found preserved initial-segment architecture and trafficking-barrier function in cultured axon-carrying-dendrite neurons, but absent initial-segment homeostatic plasticity under the tested conditions, fewer cisternal organelles, and fewer inhibitory inputs. The barrier’s existence is therefore not the open question.
why: Tests whether a distinct neuronal geometry requires a distinct stability mechanism.
key_works: Han et al. (2025), *Unveiling the cell biology of hippocampal neurons with dendritic axon origin*, DOI: `10.1083/jcb.202403141`; Thome et al. (2014), *Axon-Carrying Dendrites Convey Privileged Synaptic Input in Hippocampal Neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2014.08.013`.

title: R10.13. Dynamic regulation of the periaxonal nanocircuit
open: Measure how the nanoscale space between axon and myelin changes in geometry and ionic composition during realistic spike trains. Determine whether those changes actively regulate conduction or instead create activity-dependent failure and timing noise.
status: A 2020 study combined recordings, ultrastructure, and modeling to establish a conductive periaxonal pathway in saltatory conduction. Its existence does not settle whether nanospace width and conductivity are dynamically controlled during behavior.
why: Identifies a potential regulator of axonal timing that is distinct from changing myelin thickness or internode length.
key_works: Cohen et al. (2020), *Saltatory Conduction along Myelinated Axons Involves a Periaxonal Nanocircuit*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.11.039`.

title: R10.14. Replenishment and fate of the adult silent-filopodial synapse reserve
open: Determine whether adult filopodial silent synapses are continuously replenished, consumed by learning, recycled, or converted into long-lived spines. Quantify the reserve’s turnover and test whether its depletion limits subsequent learning.
status: In 2022, filopodia were identified as a major substrate of silent synapses in sampled adult mouse visual-cortical neurons, and their functional recruitment was demonstrated. The unresolved issue is the reserve’s long-term lifecycle, not whether adult silent synapses exist.
why: Could reveal a renewable structural resource supporting adult learning.
key_works: Vardalaki, Chung, and Harnett (2022), *Filopodia are a structural substrate for silent synapses in adult neocortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05483-6`.

title: R10.15. Regulation of opposing transmitters inside the same vesicle
open: Determine how the glutamate-to-GABA content of individual co-packaged vesicles is established and whether it changes with activity or physiological state. Predict when a release event produces net excitation, inhibition, or a timing-dependent combination at its target.
status: A 2022 study demonstrated co-packaging of glutamate and GABA in individual vesicles at a defined central synapse. Thus, co-packaging itself is not hypothetical; its stoichiometric regulation and functional flexibility are the finer-grained targets.
why: Challenges models that assign a single fixed sign to a presynaptic release event.
key_works: Kim et al. (2022), *Co-packaging of opposing neurotransmitters in individual synaptic vesicles in the central nervous system*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.01.007`; Kim and Sabatini (2023), *Analytical approaches to examine gamma-aminobutyric acid and glutamate vesicular co-packaging*, DOI: `10.3389/fnsyn.2022.1076616`.

title: R10.16. Arc capsid cargo selection and recipient specificity
open: Identify which endogenous RNAs are preferentially packaged into Arc particles, which cells receive them, and what transferred cargo does in those recipients. Separate intercellular transfer functions from Arc’s intracellular roles using interventions that preserve one while disrupting the other.
status: In 2018, Arc was shown to form virus-like capsids and mediate intercellular RNA transfer. These findings do not establish a complete endogenous cargo-selection code or prove which behavioral effects require transfer between cells.
why: Could identify a genetically encoded communication channel distinct from neurotransmission.
key_works: Pastuzyn et al. (2018), *The Neuronal Gene Arc Encodes a Repurposed Retrotransposon Gag Protein that Mediates Intercellular RNA Transfer*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2017.12.024`.

title: R10.17. Identities and receptors of neuronal membrane-proteasome peptides
open: Identify the physiologically released peptides produced by neuronal membrane proteasomes and establish which receptors or uptake mechanisms mediate their effects. Distinguish direct receptor binding from indirect changes in glutamate signaling or extracellular protein processing.
status: Work published in 2024 linked membrane-proteasome-derived peptides to NMDAR-dependent signaling and gene-expression changes; another study implicated membrane proteasomes in peripheral nociceptor activity. NMDAR dependence does not establish that the peptides directly bind NMDARs.
why: Could uncover a signaling system whose molecular messages remain inadequately identified.
key_works: Türker, Brennan, and Margolis (2024), *Neuronal membrane proteasome-derived peptides modulate NMDAR-dependent neuronal signaling to promote changes in gene expression*, DOI: `10.1091/mbc.E23-06-0218`; Villalón Landeros et al. (2024), *The nociceptive activity of peripheral sensory neurons is modulated by the neuronal membrane proteasome*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114058`.

title: R10.20. The last reversible state after SARM1 activation
open: Define the biochemical and electrophysiological boundary beyond which an axon cannot recover after SARM1 activation. Determine how that boundary changes with injury type, neuronal subtype, and duration, using restoration of conduction and synaptic output rather than survival alone.
status: A 2025 human-neuron study demonstrated reversible mitochondrial dysfunction after SARM1 activation and protection through antisense intervention. Reversibility is therefore already demonstrated in a defined setting; the open target is a predictive, transferable rescue window and proof of complete functional recovery.
why: Establishes when intervention can still rescue an existing axon rather than merely delay fragmentation.
key_works: Loreto et al. (2025), *SARM1 activation induces reversible mitochondrial dysfunction and can be prevented in human neurons by antisense oligonucleotides*, DOI: `10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106986`.

title: R10.23. The metastable visual-pigment state proposed to generate continuous dark noise
open: Identify the molecular conformation and transition kinetics of the visual-pigment state proposed to generate continuous dark noise. Predict how mutations alter this noise independently of photon sensitivity and discrete thermal activation events.
status: A 2024 study attributed an important continuous-noise component to visual pigment and proposed a metastable pigment state. The state’s detailed molecular identity remains a mechanistic target rather than a solved structural result.
why: Could explain a fundamental sensory-noise source at molecular resolution.
key_works: Chai et al. (2024), *Dark continuous noise from visual pigment as a major mechanism underlying rod–cone difference in light sensitivity*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2418031121`.

title: R10.25. The downstream use of suppressed-by-contrast retinal ganglion cells
open: Determine whether suppressed-by-contrast ganglion cells causally help distinguish self-generated visual changes from external events. Identify their downstream readers and predict behavioral consequences of selectively altering their suppression signals.
status: In 2015, a genetically identified population reliably signaled stimuli resembling saccades and blinks, with specific excitatory and inhibitory mechanisms characterized. Reliable signaling of those stimuli is established; necessity for perceptual stabilization is the remaining target.
why: Links an unusual retinal response class to a concrete computation rather than leaving it as a physiological curiosity.
key_works: Tien et al. (2015), *Genetically Identified Suppressed-by-Contrast Retinal Ganglion Cells Reliably Signal Self-Generated Visual Stimuli*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1521-15.2015`.

title: R10.27. Can artificial cone-subpopulation signals create an additional learned chromatic dimension?
open: Determine whether independently addressing subsets within a cone class can support a learned perceptual distinction that cannot be reduced to ordinary color coordinates or spatial texture. Success requires generalization across new spatial arrangements and controls that exclude brightness and pattern cues.
status: The 2025 Oz study demonstrated colors outside the ordinary natural gamut through selective cone stimulation. An expanded gamut, including the reported “olo” percept, is not by itself evidence of an additional independent dimension of color vision.
why: Tests whether adult visual processing can acquire a new sensory coordinate rather than merely experience unusually strong activation of existing coordinates.
key_works: Fong et al. (2025), *Novel color via stimulation of individual photoreceptors at population scale*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`.

title: R10.28. Tenfold scaling of individually addressed, spectrally typed cones
open: Scale controlled stimulation from roughly **10³ to 10⁴ individually typed cones**, while holding cross-activation, retinal exposure, tracking failures, and perceptual reproducibility to predefined acceptance limits. This is a proposed engineering target, not a published performance claim.
status: The 2025 Oz prototype operated at approximately the thousand-cone scale and demonstrated image and video stimuli. Scaling spatial coverage without losing cone-level targeting is a different problem from demonstrating the initial percept.
why: Would make richer tests of neural adaptation to artificial sensory channels possible.
key_works: Fong et al. (2025), the Oz study identified in R10.27, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`.

title: R10.30. The competence boundary for PTBP1-based astrocyte reprogramming
open: Determine whether any reproducibly defined mature-astrocyte state undergoes genuine neuronal conversion after PTBP1 loss, or establish a bounded negative result across those states. Positive claims must demonstrate irreversible lineage, durable neuronal physiology, and exclusion of pre-existing neurons or labeling artifacts.
status: A 2025 study found that PTBP1 depletion in lineage-traced mature astrocytes altered splicing without broadly producing neuronal features. The next problem is not to repeat an unqualified conversion claim, but to identify the actual competence boundary—or explain why PTBP1 removal is insufficient.
why: Prevents a potentially misleading regeneration strategy from advancing on ambiguous cell-labeling evidence.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2025), *PTBP1 depletion in mature astrocytes reveals distinct splicing alterations without neuronal features*, eLife research report `107683`; preprint DOI: `10.1101/2025.05.30.657115`.

title: R10.33. Quantitative partition of central and peripheral tACS effects
open: Estimate what fraction of a transcranial alternating-current stimulation effect arises from direct brain fields versus stimulation of peripheral nerves. Predict that partition across anatomies and tasks instead of assuming that either mechanism always dominates.
status: In 2019, one study demonstrated that motor-system effects could arise through peripheral nerves, while another demonstrated entrainment of primate single-neuron activity. The useful unresolved question is context-dependent causal contribution, not a binary claim that direct or indirect effects never occur.
why: Makes stimulation results interpretable and improves targeting.
key_works: Asamoah, Khatoun, and McLaughlin (2019), *tACS motor system effects can be caused by transcutaneous stimulation of peripheral nerves*, PMID: `30655523`; Krause et al. (2019), *Transcranial alternating current stimulation entrains single-neuron activity in the primate brain*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1815958116`.

title: R10.36. Causal leaders and replacement rules in the GnRH pulse generator
open: Determine whether early-recruited kisspeptin neurons causally initiate a hormone pulse or merely report a distributed transition. Predict whether removing an apparent leader suppresses pulses, changes their timing, or causes another cell to assume its role.
status: In-vivo imaging in 2022 revealed temporal recruitment order within the pulse generator, and subsequent work examined synchronization mechanisms. Observed ordering does not by itself establish a fixed pacemaker hierarchy or its resilience to cell loss.
why: Distinguishes a replaceable distributed oscillator from a small set of indispensable initiators.
key_works: Moore et al. (2022), *In vivo imaging of the GnRH pulse generator reveals a temporal order of neuronal activation and synchronization during each pulse*, PMID: `35110409`; Han et al. (2023), *Mechanism of kisspeptin neuron synchronization for pulsatile hormone secretion in male mice*, Cell Reports 42, article `111914`.

title: R10.38. The molecular message from cerebrospinal fluid to skull marrow
open: Identify which cerebrospinal-fluid molecules instruct particular skull-marrow progenitors and immune-cell populations after a defined neural injury. Determine whether the resulting response preserves spatial information about the injury or is simply a generalized inflammatory signal.
status: Direct cerebrospinal-fluid access to skull bone-marrow niches through dural channels, together with injury-associated marrow responses, was demonstrated in 2022. The route exists; the unresolved target is the specific message, recipient program, and distinction from circulating signals.
why: Could make local neuroimmune recruitment selectively controllable without suppressing systemic immunity.
key_works: Mazzitelli et al. (2022), *Cerebrospinal fluid regulates skull bone marrow niches via direct access through dural channels*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-022-01029-1`.

title: R10.39. Biological learning versus decoder adaptation in cultured-neuron computing
open: Determine how much task improvement comes from changes inside living neural tissue rather than adaptation of an electronic decoder, fixed reservoir dynamics, or changes in stimulation statistics. Require fixed-readout and matched-control conditions, plus selective disruption of the proposed biological plasticity mechanism.
status: DishBrain in 2022 and Brainoware in 2023 reported task-relevant behavior or computation using living neural preparations. These demonstrations motivate—but do not replace—a causal accounting of which component learned and what was retained. Claims about “sentience” are not required to formulate or solve this technical problem.
why: Establishes whether living tissue provides adaptive computation beyond what a fixed nonlinear substrate and trained readout would deliver.
key_works: Kagan et al. (2022), *In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.09.001`; Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`.

title: R10.40. End-to-end efficiency advantage for living neural computing
open: Demonstrate a **proposed tenfold improvement** in energy or total operating cost per successfully completed task against a specified electronic baseline, including incubation, fluid handling, amplifiers, stimulation, training, failed cultures, and replacement. Match task accuracy, throughput, and availability rather than comparing isolated neuronal energy consumption.
status: Brainoware demonstrated organoid-based reservoir computation in 2023. That is not an end-to-end demonstration of a tenfold efficiency advantage after all supporting equipment and biological maintenance are included.
why: Determines whether biological computing has a practical advantage rather than an attractive comparison at only one system boundary.
key_works: Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`.

title: Tenfold cheaper verified connectomics
open: Reduce total acquisition, reconstruction, proofreading, storage, and access cost by at least tenfold against a preregistered baseline while maintaining measured synapse and connectivity error rates.
status: Proposed moonshot; MICrONS supplies a substantial real pipeline against which component and end-to-end improvements can be measured.
why: Makes replication across animals, conditions, and laboratories feasible.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.
